title: The cantonists
hookLine: Jewish boys are conscripted into the Russian army for a lifetime of service

lines: SONGS SO A CHILD WILL BE REMEMBERED.
cards: Some songs are sung so a child will fall asleep. Others are sung so a child will be remembered.

In the Yiddish-speaking towns of the Russian Empire, there were songs of the second kind: a boy snatched from his bed at night, a mother running after a wagon, men who came for the children of the poor.
They are memories set to a tune, about a real law and real boys. A gentle warning: today is about children taken from their families.

teach.b: Under Tsar Nicholas the First, the Russian Empire began drafting Jews into its army, and it did something especially cruel with Jewish boys.
Boys not yet old enough to be soldiers could be taken anyway and sent to military schools for soldiers' children, called cantonist schools, often far from home.
The service that followed was so long that a boy taken as a child might come home a grown man, if he came home at all.
In those schools, boys were pressed, sometimes brutally, to be baptized and leave Judaism behind. Some held on. Some could not.
And part of this story is painful to tell, and Jewish memory tells it honestly.

teach.h: A QUOTA THE COMMUNITY HAD TO FILL.
teach.b: The empire made each Jewish community hand over its own quota of recruits, so the choosing fell on the community's leaders.

Too often, the sons of the poor and the orphans were handed over, and men called khappers, snatchers, were hired to seize boys when families hid them. The wound ran outward, against the empire, and inward too.

The prophet Jeremiah gave this grief its words: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not."
Rachel, the matriarch, weeping for children who are gone.
And the next verse answers her: "they shall come again from the land of the enemy." Some cantonists did come back, some having kept their faith in secret all those years.
Their stories, and the songs, are how a people refused to let those boys be forgotten.

how: The cantonists are remembered in Yiddish songs, memoirs and later histories, and some Jewish families still tell stories of ancestors who were taken or who hid their sons.

games.q: you lead a Jewish community, and the empire demands a number of recruits from you. what does the history say happened?
o: leaders refused, and no one was taken.

practice: Bring to mind one boy from this story; you don't know his name, and that's all right, just let him be real for a moment.

Then widen your attention to children today taken from their families, by war, by law, by people who should have protected them, and simply refuse, for this moment, to forget them. If you pray, you can hold them there.
